articles.title: Your AI Outreach Read "No" as "Yes": Classify Replies Before the Next Step (n8n / Make, 2026)
articles.excerpt: Why does my AI email automation treat "no" as "yes"? Short answer: because the sequence is usually wired to advance on any reply. The AI writes a polite follow-up, and the workflow treats "a reply arr…
articles.body: Why does my AI email automation treat "no" as "yes"? Short answer: because the sequence is usually wired to advance on any reply. The AI writes a polite follow-up, and the workflow treats "a reply arrived" as "the person agreed". The fix is a small gate between the inbound reply and the next step: classify the reply into a fixed set of intents, stop the sequence on "no" or "stop", send anything unclear to a human, and only advance on an explicit yes. Default to not advancing. This came up in r/automation on 18 November 2026.
articles.author: Viet Automation

articles.title: Webhook Engineering: Retries, Dynamic Backoff, and Multi-Tenant Failure Recovery
articles.excerpt: Building a high-throughput webhook delivery engine means handling remote failures gracefully. When you deliver millions of webhooks a day to thousands of customer endpoints, naive retry loops, such as…
articles.body: Building a high-throughput webhook delivery engine means handling remote failures gracefully. When you deliver millions of webhooks a day to thousands of customer endpoints, naive retry loops, such as one exponential backoff schedule applied to every HTTP error, lead to worker starvation, retry storms and duplicated side effects. There is no single retry standard to copy. Stripe retries a live-mode event for up to three days with exponential backoff, and test-mode events are retried three times over a few hours. GitHub does not automatically redeliver failed deliveries at all. Shopify documents up to eight retries over roughly four hours and may remove the subscription if failures persist. Provider timeouts also differ: GitHub expects a 2xx within 10 seconds and Shopify within 5.

articles.title: What Are You Actually Approving When an AI Workflow Runs?
articles.excerpt: When an AI workflow runs, you should be able to say exactly what was approved: which version, which apps it may change, and whose access each call uses. Dittoly makes a person approve that exact versi…
articles.body: When an AI workflow runs, you should be able to say exactly what was approved: which version, which apps it may change, and whose access each call uses. Dittoly makes a person approve that exact version, names every identity before the first run, and needs a new approval for any edit. I built Dittoly because every AI automation demo I sat through ended the same way. An agent with 14 tools merged the right branches on stage, and someone asked to point it at production by Friday. Nobody in that room could say what they would be approving. A prompt, a tool list and a service account do not describe what will happen on Tuesday. Dittoly is open source under Apache 2.0: the project site gives the short tour, and the code is on GitHub .

articles.title: This AI Reads Scary Letters So You Don't Have To (and It Costs Less Than a Penny)
articles.excerpt: 🔬 Project Overview A lot of the people I love get letters they can't fully read. A bill from a medical billing company, a notice from the school, something from the county. The letter is in English,…
articles.body: 🔬 Project Overview A lot of the people I love get letters they can't fully read. A bill from a medical billing company, a notice from the school, something from the county. The letter is in English, the deadline is real, and the usual fix is a photo sent to someone on WhatsApp with "¿qué dice esto?". So I built CartaFácil : you open a link on your phone, take a photo of the letter, and a few seconds later you get a plain-Spanish explanation. Who sent it, what they decided, the date and the amount in big letters, what you have to do, what to bring, the phone number as a "tap to call" button, and (this one matters more than I expected) any free help the letter offers, like an interpreter or a payment plan. The first real test wasn't a sample. It was a medical bill I had at home.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Hayabusa was supposed to return asteroid samples to Earth. Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system. We study asteroids to learn more about the solar system's history. Hayabusa (pronounced HI-uh-BOOS-uh) made two touchdowns on asteroid Itokawa (EE -toh-KA-wah). Each time, the spacecraft went into safe mode. Controllers weren't sure if Hayabusa gathered any material. But they sent the spacecraft back to Earth anyway. Hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010 . Scientists found dust of Itokawa inside the capsule, proving that it did indeed capture samples of Itokawa.

articles.title: No more asteroid landing: Engine trouble forces Japan's Hayabusa2 probe to change plans
articles.excerpt: Japan's space agency has decided to switch destinations and objectives for the final act of its Hayabusa2 asteroid mission, due to problems with the spacecraft's ion thrusters.
articles.body: Japan's space agency has decided to switch destinations and objectives for the final act of its Hayabusa2 mission, due to the spacecraft suffering trouble with its ion thrusters. The veteran Hayabusa2 spacecraft launched back in 2014 to collect material from the asteroid Ryugu . Since delivering the samples to Earth in December 2020 via a reentry capsule, the main spacecraft has been conducting an extended mission of exploration and in July made a super-close flyby of the two-headed asteroid Torifune. But Hayabusa2's continued adventures are now set for a premature end.

articles.title: China rolls out rocket for launch of 1st international astronaut to Tiangong space station (video)
articles.excerpt: China has rolled to the launch pad the rocket and spacecraft for its Shenzhou-24 mission, which will fly the first international astronaut to the nation's Tiangong space station.
articles.body: China's space station is set to receive its first foreign astronaut. A Long March 2F rocket, topped with the Shenzhou-24 crew spacecraft, was rolled out to the pad at Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China, on Tuesday (Nov. 17), with launch expected in the next week. The 191-foot-tall (58 meters) rocket was transferred 0.93 miles (1.5 kilometers) from a vertical integration building to the pad over the course of around two hours, starting around 4 a.m. EST (0900 GMT, or 5 p.m. Beijing Time), according to China Central Television (CCTV). China rolls out the Long March 2F rocket for its Shenzhou-24 astronaut mission on Nov. 17, 2026.
